introduction: On this Sunday, God tells his people, Be holy, for I am holy, and commands them not to hate or take revenge but to love their neighbor as themselves. In the Gospel, Jesus goes further: love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, so that you may be children of your Father in heaven. Paul reminds us that we are God's temple. Let us ask for hearts that love as God loves.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Brothers and sisters, the Lord is merciful and gracious. Let us bring him our prayers.
intentions: For the Church: that she may witness to the love that does not seek revenge. Let us pray to the Lord.
For nations and peoples caught in cycles of violence: that they may find the courage to forgive and make peace. Let us pray to the Lord.
For our enemies and those who have hurt us: that God may bless them. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who are persecuted: that they may be strengthened by Christ's love. Let us pray to the Lord.
For ourselves: that we may be perfect in love, as our heavenly Father is perfect. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Lord God, you make your sun rise on the evil and the good. Give us hearts like yours, so that we may love our enemies and pray for those who persecute us. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: Love your enemies
reflection.body:
In the first reading, God gives his people the reason for all his commandments: "You shall be holy; for I, the LORD your God, am holy." Holiness means being like God. And this holiness is shown in how we treat others: "You shall not hate your brother in your heart," and "You shall not take vengeance, nor bear any grudge." Instead, "you shall love your neighbor as yourself."

In the Gospel, Jesus takes this teaching further. The old law of "an eye for an eye" was meant to limit revenge: the punishment could not be greater than the harm. But Jesus asks his disciples not to seek revenge at all: "whoever strikes you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also." He asks for generosity beyond what is required: if someone forces you to go one mile, "go with him two."

Then comes the hardest teaching of all: "love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you." Jesus is not asking us to feel warm emotions toward those who hurt us, or to pretend that evil is good. He is asking us to want what is good for them, and to pray for them.

Why? Because this is how God loves: "he makes his sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the just and the unjust." Loving only those who love us is easy; even "the tax collectors do the same." Jesus ends with a call that seems impossible: "Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect." We cannot do this by our own strength, but only by God's grace.

Paul reminds us who we are: "you are God's temple and... God's Spirit lives in you."

This week, pray by name for someone who has hurt you or whom you find difficult. Ask God to bless them. And refuse, at least once, to answer an offense with another offense.
